description:
Aurora is a group of passionate developers and problem-solvers who are also competitive programmers. We have a strong backend focus and experience in ML, software development, rapid prototyping.

For "The Next Frontier," we want to turn open NASA data into a working tool that is easy to understand.
summary:
South Pole Visualizer is an interactive web tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare Moon south pole landing sites and dates in seconds.

We combined NASA LOLA terrain data with NASA SPICE ephemeris to show where the Sun and Earth sit above the real terrain horizon at eight Artemis III candidate sites. Users explore the pole in 3D, move through any hour from 2027 to 2028, and see sunlight, Earth link, time until sunset or Earthset, and available solar power.

The key idea is pre-calculation. A Python pipeline computes Sun and Earth positions, lunar libration, terrain skylines and a ranking of every site for every landing date ahead of time, and saves them as compact files. The browser only reads them, so the app responds instantly and needs no server.

The ranking scores each site over a 14-day stay and gives a clear verdict with warnings for long darkness or lost Earth contact. This matters because at the south pole a small change in site or date can decide whether a lander has power and a link to Earth.
details:
Lunar South Pole Visualizer lets users evaluate lunar landing sites near the south pole. For each site it shows if the Sun and Earth are above the local horizon, how long until sunset or Earthset, the Sun and Earth visibility for the next 14 and 30 days, and a ranking of the sites for a chosen landing date. The Moon, Earth and Sun are shown in 3D with true sizes and distances. The true terrain can be shown as a height heatmap. A radar view shows where the Sun and Earth are in the sky and where the terrain blocks them. A video-style time bar lets users move through time. It works on desktop and phone.

Two kinds of data are combined. The Sun and Earth move (dynamic), and the terrain horizon does not (static). We read NASA SPICE kernels with Python (SpiceyPy) and pre-calculate the Sun, Earth and Moon positions and the Moon's orientation for every hour into one small file (17 numbers per hour, 1.19 MB). From the NASA LOLA terrain, we measure the skyline of each site in 720 directions once. In the browser, checking if the Sun is visible is only a lookup, so it is instant. The 685 MB terrain file is cut into small tiles, so only the south pole part is used and the page stays light. The ranking is rule-based: 50% Sun, 30% Earth, 20% continuity of light, and a site is NO-GO if the Sun is visible less than 25% of the time. We did not use machine learning, because there is nothing to predict: the exact sky positions and the exact skyline are known, so visibility is a direct calculation.

Engineers get numbers they can check. Educators get a clear 3D picture of how the Sun, Earth and Moon move and why the pole is special. The public gets an easy tool that opens in the browser with no install.

A quick way for anyone to understand why the south pole is hard, and to compare landing sites before looking at detailed mission analysis. The ranking is a planning aid, not a full mission analysis.

JavaScript, Three.js (WebGL, shaders), HTML/CSS; Python, SpiceyPy, NumPy; NASA SPICE kernels and NASA LOLA LDEM terrain data.
